queue.tree_name: Yang Na of the City Pillar, Wat Chedi Luang
queue.recognise: You can recognise it by its size, 30 metres tall and 6 metres round. It stands in the courtyard of Wat Chedi Luang beside the shrine of the Inthakin city pillar; another yang na may stand close by.
queue.story:
This tree was planted to mark a city. When King Kawila resettled Chiang Mai in the reign that ran from 1782 to 1813, a yang na went into the ground beside the Inthakin, the city pillar, as its partner. In Thai it is a ton mai mai mueang, a tree that marks the city.

Thailand's Ministry of Culture lists it among its Heritage Trees of the Land as Yang Na Rom Mongkhon, 30 metres tall and 6 metres round, and gives its age as 200 years. Chiang Mai News put it at 226 in 2026, and an older count says about 210. None comes from counting rings, so somewhere between 200 and 230 is the honest figure.

queue.tree_name: Ardkinglas Silver Fir, the Mightiest Conifer
queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, nearly ten metres round, which splits into several large stems. It stands in the Ardkinglas woodland garden; the estate does not publish the spot, so our pin marks the garden.
queue.story:
The Ardkinglas estate calls this the mightiest conifer in Europe, and the trunk makes the case. It is a silver fir with a girth of nearly ten metres by the estate's measure, over 31 feet by Wikipedia's. The name is not new. It was given, the estate says, by the 10th Duke of Argyll more than a hundred years ago.

The estate puts it at about 250 years old. That is the owner's figure, and the only one we have, so read it as a claim rather than a count. Accounts describe the trunk dividing into several great stems, so expect a mass of timber rather than a single column.

What is missing is just as plain. No height is published. The estate does not say where in the garden it stands, so our pin ma

queue.recognise: You can recognise it as the tallest conifer in the lower woodland garden, the Pinetum, about 64 metres high and five metres round. It stands along the Window Walk above the water, a few minutes from the lochan and the weir bridge.
queue.story:
For a number of years this was the tallest tree in Britain, the Ardkinglas estate says. The grand fir went into the lower woodland garden, the Pinetum, as a sapling around 1875. By 2002 it was recorded at 203 feet. A climber measured it at 64.28 metres in 2010, a walk report in 2014 gave 63.4, and the estate's own figure, from July 2025, is 64.8 metres. Different methods give different answers at this height, so call it around 64 metres.

The title has since moved north. The estate itself credits a Douglas fir in Reelig Glen, near Inverness, measured at 66.4 metres, with taking it, and says the record changed hands three times in a single year. Ardkinglas keeps the grand fir on its list of c

queue.recognise: You can recognise it as the large fig on the west side of the South Pasadena Public Library. It stands in Library Park, beside the library building.
queue.story:
South Pasadena's Landmark No. 55 is not a house or a storefront. It is a fig planted by a man from the city's street department. The city council added the Moreton Bay fig beside the public library to its Historic Landmark Register in December 2018.

The South Pasadenan dates the planting to 1930, which would make the fig about 95 years old. The sources do not quite line up. A second piece in the same paper, from 2011, said only that it went in about 80 years earlier, which lands in the same years, while one writer guessed at a century without saying why. The 1930 date has the better footing.

queue.recognise: You can recognise them by the pair of giant sequoias, 27 and 29 metres, the tallest trees on the campus. They stand over the Boole Library at University College Cork.
queue.story: The tallest trees on University College Cork's campus were paid for with beer. William Crawford of the Beamish & Crawford brewery, one of the young college's great benefactors, donated the pair of Giant Redwoods that now stand 27 and 29 metres above the Boole Library, and at roughly 150 years old they have barely started: in California's Sierra Nevada the species passes 2,000 years and 80 metres. They are the obvious landmarks of a campus that is quietly one of Ireland's best tree collections, planted continuously since the college opened in 1849 and accredited as an arboretum by the international ArbNet programme in 2020, around 2,500 trees of some 120 species. queue.tree_name: The Variegated Maple of Coevorden Castle
queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the leaves, splashed and streaked with cream rather than plain green. It is the maple on the open ground in front of Kasteel Coevorden.
queue.story:
From across the grounds this maple looks as though somebody is shining a light on it.

That is the cultivar. 'Leopoldii' is a sycamore whose leaves come out flecked and streaked with cream, yellow and pink instead of plain green, so a whole tree of it reads as permanently dappled. Nurseries pushed variegated forms hard in the nineteenth century, when one of them on a good lawn was a statement rather than a plant.

This one went into the ground between 1880 and 1890, on the most conspicuous spot at Kasteel Coevorden, and it still frames the view of the building.

queue.recognise: You can recognise it by its chestnut brown bark curling back by itself to show a glossy copper red layer underneath. It stands in the National Botanic Gardens, Glasnevin.
queue.story: The bark peels away by itself here, in curling chestnut strips that show a glossy copper red layer underneath. Arbutus x andrachnoides is a naturally occurring hybrid from the Mediterranean, a cross between the familiar strawberry tree and the smooth-barked Arbutus andrachne of Greece and Cyprus, and it takes after the more dramatic parent: a colour show that has nothing to do with flowers or leaves. The Tree Council of Ireland's 2009 heritage survey lists a specimen of this hybrid among the National Botanic Gardens' Exceptional Specimen Trees, aged 100 to 150 years then, roughly 120 to 165 now. queue.tree_name: The Twin Cypresses of the Parador
queue.recognise: You can recognise them by the pair, two cypresses standing one on either side of a doorway. They flank what was once the entrance to the royal tombs, in the Parador garden reached from the cafe and restaurant terrace.
queue.story: Two centenarian cypresses flank what was once the entrance to a set of royal tombs, inside a garden that has spent the last five centuries as a Franciscan convent, then a hotel. The Parador de Granada occupies the former Convento de San Francisco, built in the 15th century within the Alhambra's own walls, on ground the Catholic Monarchs Ferdinand and Isabella briefly chose as their own burial place before their remains moved to the Royal Chapel in the city below. queue.story:
Malta calls this the thousand-year-old carob, and the best evidence for that number may be a poem. A local guide says the figure comes from verses on the dry-stone wall beneath the tree. Lovin Malta repeated it in 2021, describing the tree as dated around 1,000 years without saying how, and the community map of the island lists it as a natural monument of the same age.

Nobody has dated it properly, so read the thousand as a local claim. What has been measured is the trunk. A trail leaflet from 2006 gives it a girth of 7.25 metres across its several stems, and a carob that size has been growing for several hundred years at least. queue.tree_name: The Gnarled Beech of Hampstead Heath
queue.recognise: A veteran beech in woodland on Hampstead Heath with a large dark hollow split open at its base, a fluted grey trunk and a low rope fence around it.
queue.story:
The base of this beech has split open into a dark hollow you could crouch inside, and above it the trunk rises fluted and buttressed into a fan of heavy limbs. A reader standing at it on Hampstead Heath in autumn sent it to us with three words: "Amazing gnarley trunk". The photograph backs them up.

Old beeches age like this. Their bark stays smooth but the wood inside rots away, the base opens up, and the tree carries on as a shell, often for a long time. This one still has a full crown turning gold, and the ground around it is deep in its own leaves.

We have no name for it, no age and no measurement, and no register we checked lists it. The Heath has many veteran beeches, so look for the

queue.recognise: You can recognise it as a low, mossy wood of twisted oaks among granite boulders on the hillside above the West Dart. It is about a 25 minute walk north of the Two Bridges car park, seen from the path along its edge.
queue.story:
Around 1620 a visitor described the oaks of Wistman's Wood as no taller than a man could reach the top of with his head. Four centuries later most of them still rarely pass 4.5 metres. They grow at 380 to 410 metres up on the open moor above the West Dart, rooted among granite boulders, low, twisted and thick with moss.

This is a wood, not a tree, and the wood is the destination. It covers about 3.5 hectares in three groves, North, Middle and South. The oldest oaks appear to be 400 to 500 years old; one felled in 1866 turned out to be about 168. queue.recognise: You can recognise it as the wide oak, about five metres round, alone where several rides meet. It stands in Epping Forest just north of Connaught Water.
queue.story:
This oak has three names, and the sources disagree on which came first. It was the Cuckoo Oak, and it is also Bedford's Oak, after J T Bedford, the City of London councillor who fought in the 1870s to save the Forest. OpenStreetMap and the walking guides call it Grimston's Oak, after the cricketer Robert Grimston, who lived from 1816 to 1884. The Epping Forest Heritage Trust treats Bedford's and Grimston's as one and the same tree.

Whatever you call it, it has been a landmark for at least three centuries. An engraving from the 1870s shows it looking much as it does now, standing alone where several forest rides meet just north of Connaught Water. The Trust puts its age at possibly 400 years

queue.tree_name: The Plane Trees of the Circus
queue.recognise: Five planes on the enclosed green at the centre of the circle, their crowns now higher than the roofline of the terraces around them.
queue.story: The Circus is three curved terraces of Grade I listed townhouses arranged into a full circle, John Wood the Elder's answer to the Colosseum and one of the defining images of Georgian Bath. For its first decades the ring at the centre was paved stone setts sitting over a reservoir that supplied the surrounding houses with water. In 1800 the residents enclosed that centre as a private garden, grassed it over, and planted five London Planes, reportedly to cut down on the dust that horse-drawn carriages kicked up on the surrounding road. queue.tree_name: The Orange Courtyard of the Mezquita
queue.recognise: You can recognise it by its rows of orange trees lined up with the columns of the prayer hall next door, linked by shallow water channels. It stands as the Patio de los Naranjos.
queue.story: Ninety-eight bitter orange trees stand here in rows that line up with the columns of the prayer hall next door, so the courtyard reads as the building continuing outdoors into the light. It may be the oldest surviving garden in Europe. The enclosure goes back to the mosque founded in 784, orange trees are recorded in it from at least 1512, and the shallow channels that link the tree pits still carry the water that feeds them. In 2001 workers found a tenth-century cistern twelve metres beneath the paving, built to hold twelve hundred cubic metres so that washing and irrigation would never stop. queue.recognise: You can recognise them as the pair of big yews at the ruins of Old Crom Castle, said to mark the old garden entrance. The larger is 474 cm round near the ground, the smaller 430 cm; our pin is approximate.
queue.story:
Two yews at Crom are said to have marked the entrance to a castle garden that has not existed since the 1760s. The old castle was built in 1611, during the Plantation of Ulster, and burnt in the early 1760s. Today they stand at the ruins on the Crom estate, on Upper Lough Erne, and the garden they once flanked is gone.

Nobody knows how old they are, and the claims are wide. Lord Erne is said to put them at 800 years. A National Trust trail guide, by a summary we could not read in full, gives anything from 400 to 1,000, and the Trust itself admits the debate has run for years. We leave the age open. The earliest written mention we found is J.C. Loudon's, in 1837.

That is tradition rather than a count of rings, and it is worth saying so, but the measurements are consistent with an old tree: 782 centimetres round at chest height when it was last measured in 2019, over thirty four metres tall, with a crown spreading forty three metres. queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, about 8.5 metres round, beside the boardwalk in Village Point Park Preserve. It stands in Daphne, on the eastern shore of Mobile Bay.
queue.story:
Andrew Jackson is supposed to have stood under this oak in 1814 and addressed his troops on the way to Pensacola. That is the local legend, and it stays a legend. No document puts Jackson at this tree, and the Encyclopedia of Alabama's caption says only that he reportedly did.

The tree needs no help from him. Gulf Coast Media gave the trunk as 28 feet around in 2023, about 8.5 metres, and was careful to add that it is not Alabama's champion live oak, because an oak in Mobile County beats it by roughly two feet. queue.recognise: You can recognise it as the fenced pear beside the North Shore Medical Center parking lot, the old tree behind the fence. The 2011 historic marker stands at the viewing point above the lot.
queue.story:
The oldest living cultivated fruit tree in North America grows beside a hospital car park in Danvers, about 25 kilometres north of Boston. It is a pear, planted sometime between 1632 and about 1640 by John Endecott, governor of the Massachusetts Bay Colony, and it is the only survivor of his orchard.

It has had a hard four centuries. It came through a storm in 1770. In 1952 a CBS-Hytron plant and its parking lot went up around it until it was nearly hidden. In 1964 vandals took a hacksaw to its branches and trunk and cut it down to about six feet. It grew back. queue.recognise: You can recognise it by its hollow trunk, roughly half of it gone, leaning toward the fountain beside it. It stands in the Patio de los Naranjos at the Mezquita-Catedral.
queue.story: This tree is on a map drawn in 1741, which is a rarer thing than being old. Most claims about an ancient tree's age come from tradition; this one comes from an inventory of the courtyard that counted, alongside the olive, ninety-five orange trees, six cypresses, ten palms and a chinaberry. Two and a half centuries later roughly half its trunk is gone. It hollowed through the twentieth century, decayed badly from the 1980s, and what leans toward the fountain now is a shell that still manages about sixty kilos of olives a year. queue.story:
A dawn redwood stands on a lawn of the Préfargier park in La Tène, and a reader photographed it in its autumn colour, the whole crown burnt orange against a pale blue sky. They named it a métaséquoia, the French name for Metasequoia, and gave a girth of 250 centimetres.

A gravel path runs along the bottom of the frame. The dawn redwood sheds its needles each year, which is unusual for a conifer, and the orange phase lasts only a few weeks.

queue.recognise: A huge tent of drooping beech branches on an open lawn, reaching almost to the ground.
queue.story:
Three weeping beeches grow together on a lawn of the Préfargier park in La Tène, and their drooping branches have joined into one huge curtain of leaves that reaches almost to the ground. A reader photographed them in autumn with the single note “3 hêtres pleureurs”, three weeping beeches.

In the photograph the mass of leaves is many times the height of the visitor who stands under its edge, green with yellow and gold at the tips. Behind it the other trees are in orange autumn colour.

We found no register entry, girth or planting date, so this page gives none. A weeping beech is a cultivated form of the common beech, grown for its hanging shoots, and it grows into just this kind of tent.

queue.story:
A reader photographed a great pedunculate oak in an open field on Clingoe Hill in Greenstead, on the east side of Colchester. Their app listed it as an oak near Mistley, but the GPS fix puts it in Colchester, and we have placed it there. They gave a girth of 600 centimetres and an age of about 300 years.

The photograph shows a tree that fills the frame. The crown is a full, rounded dome of dark green leaves, and under it a short, wide trunk with deep hollows and burrs at head height. Two people stand at its foot, one with arms spread wide against the bark, and they look small. The grass around it is dry and pale, the crown still green, so the picture was taken in a dry late summer.

queue.recognise: A tall ginkgo in the garden beside the campus library, its two crowns turning one bright yellow in autumn.
queue.story:
A ginkgo in the garden of the library at the Carmarthen campus of the University of Wales Trinity Saint David turns a deep gold each autumn, and a reader sent us a photograph of it in the rain. The library has large glass windows that look onto the garden, and the reader says that in autumn the tree “shines its glory through those windows.”

In the photograph two crowns rise together out of one mass of leaves, every one the same bright yellow, against a grey sky. A white balcony and a slope of roof sit at the left edge of the frame, the grass below is green, and a few leaves are already on the ground.
